Date: 2026-01-10 | Start: 16:32 UTC | Duration: 47m | Recording: Enabled
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Zetta Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (VP Eng), Aisha Khan (SecOps)

summary: Discovery focused on per-token unit economics and deployment tradeoffs (hosted / dedicated / private). Zetta is cost-sensitive, running a multimodal product with peaks during business hours and strict data residency for some PII. Key asks: side-by-side cost scenarios for expected traffic, practical batching and KV cache recommendations to hit a sub-200ms p95 latency for short conversations, and an outline of compliance controls for private deployments.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya Menon: Priya here, head of ML at Zetta. Hi all.
[00:10] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos, VP Eng, good to meet you.
[00:13] Aisha Khan: Aisha, SecOps.
[00:15] Marcus Patel: Marcus from Redwood, SE on the call.
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: Cool. Agenda is short — cost/unit econ, deploy mode tradeoffs, and next steps for a pilot if we align.
[00:30] Priya Menon: Great. I'll start with context — we're running a multimodal assistant, mainly text with occasional embeddings for retrieval. Monthly token volumes today are around 400M but growing fast, and our peaks hit ~120 qps during US business hrs. Our budget for inference is tight — want to keep marginal token cost under ~$0.0008 ideally.
[01:05] Marcus Patel: Thanks Priya. Two quick clarifying Qs — what's your 95th latency SLA target and how long are typical prompts/outputs?
[01:12] Priya Menon: Target p95 is 200ms for short interactions (under 80 tokens out), but we can tolerate 800-1k ms for longer generations. Typical prompts are 20-60 input tokens with 30-120 output tokens depending on task.
[01:27] Carlos Ruiz: Also data residency: some of the training prompts and user PII must stay in EU. So if we go hosted, need EU region only or private.
[01:36] Lena Ortiz: Got it. Region and latency are primary constraints. On pricing and unit econ, Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private. Marcus, want to walk through how we think about per-token and operational levers?
[01:46] Marcus Patel: Sure. High level — there are three levers to hit marginal cost and latency targets: model selection/quantization, batching and KV caching, and deployment topology (hosted shared pool vs dedicated GPU vs private on-prem). For your 400M monthly tokens with peaks at 120 qps, dedicated often helps if you want predictable latency and lower unit cost at scale, but hosted is simplest to start.
[02:10] Priya Menon: Can you quantify "lower unit cost" — ballpark numbers for hosted vs dedicated?
[02:16] Marcus Patel: Ballpark and very approximate — hosted per-token might be $0.0010 to $0.0015 depending on model; dedicated committed capacity can bring that down 30–50% depending on utilization and quantization. So if hosted is $0.001, dedicated could be $0.0005–0.0007. But those numbers vary by sequence length and batching efficiency.
[02:42] Carlos Ruiz: Does Redwood do prefix caching or KV cache? Our workload has a lot of repeated system prompts and shared context among similar sessions.
[02:50] Marcus Patel: Yes, we do prefix and KV cache. For chat flows with repeated system tokens, effective per-token cost drop can be 15–35% because cached tokens don't re-decode. CAVEAT: caching benefits depend on session stickiness and the fraction of repeated tokens. Also our automatic prefix caching may be imperfect for retrieval-augmented sequences — some of that gets tricky.
[03:14] Aisha Khan: How does batching affect latency — we worry about batching increasing p95 beyond our 200ms target.
[03:20] Marcus Patel: Good callout. Continuous batching improves throughput and reduces cost per token but can increase tail latency if you wait too long to fill a batch. In Hosted we tune batching to respect latency SLOs; you can configure a max wait time or target batch size. On Dedicated, you get control to set batching aggressiveness; if you need hard p95 <200ms, we can set low max-wait (e.g., 3–8ms) and rely on more GPUs or smaller batch sizes. That increases unit cost though.
[03:53] Priya Menon: For our use case, short interactions need the strict p95. Could caching alone help avoid higher cost?
[03:59] Marcus Patel: Potentially yes — if a large fraction of tokens are cached, you effectively reduce live decoding. Combined with quantization (8-bit / 4-bit), we can push cost down further. But quantization sometimes impacts quality — we run model-specific evals.
[04:18] Lena Ortiz: Quick note — we also have a tooling piece Redwood Optimize that suggests quantization profiles per workload and gives cost/quality tradeoffs. Marcus can share sample profiles.
[04:27] Marcus Patel: I'll add that in the follow-up.
[04:30] [05:00] Lena Ortiz: Let's do a concrete example: assume 400M tokens / month, average response 60 tokens, and 120 qps peaks. How would you recommend starting? Marcus?
[05:08] Marcus Patel: Start hosted for a short pilot to validate quality and caching behavior. For the pilot we estimate per-token host cost ~ $0.0011 with default batching. With caching engaged and a 20% cache hit rate from repeated system tokens, effective per-token cost drops to ~ $0.0009. If you commit to dedicated with 70% utilization and 4-bit quantization, you'd be in the $0.0005–0.0006 range.
[05:34] Carlos Ruiz: Those committed numbers — we assume monthly commitment? What does burst look like if we exceed capacity?
[05:40] Marcus Patel: Dedicated includes configurable burst capacity — you can reserve base throughput and allow hosted overflow for spikes, billed at hosted rates. Autoscale policies can also schedule extra GPUs for predictable peaks.
[05:50] Priya Menon: And private deployment? Our SecOps asks for VPC/on-prem options; how different are the economics there?
[05:58] Marcus Patel: Private usually has a higher fixed platform fee and ops cost but can be cheaper on variable costs if you control hardware and get large utilization. There's also integration and support overhead. For strict residency needs, private (VPC or on-prem) is the route; committed private contracts often have longer lead times.
[06:17] Aisha Khan: On compliance — does Redwood provide audit logs and KMS integration if we go private?
[06:21] Lena Ortiz: Yes — private includes KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, SSO/SAML and RBAC controls. We'll include SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[06:29] [06:45] Priya Menon: Ok, practical ask: show us three scenarios with unit econ — 1) hosted baseline with default batching, 2) hosted + caching + recommended batching tweaks, 3) dedicated committed with quantization. Also show worst-case for latency impact.
[06:44] Marcus Patel: We'll produce a small spreadsheet with per-token math, cost assumptions, and sensitivity to cache-hit rate and batch fill time.
[06:52] Carlos Ruiz: On the model side, are there Redwood-verified model performance numbers we can compare?
[06:57] Marcus Patel: Yes we publish perf profiles for models we curate; they have sequence length and throughput numbers per GPU type. Those are in the perf docs I'll link. Note transcription: sometimes the docs show K V cache as K-V cash in auto transcripts — apologies in advance.
[07:14] Priya Menon: Haha noted.
[07:17] [08:00] Carlos Ruiz: A practical technical deep-dive question — our application includes retrieval that returns snippets of user context. For reranking and embeddings we might want separate endpoints. How would batching and model selection change?
[08:10] Marcus Patel: Separate endpoints are recommended. Embeddings / rerank are usually cheap per-call but can be high volume; batching there is highly effective. For reranking, you can use smaller models and aggressive batching; generation endpoints require different latency SLOs. We can recommend mixed clusters — dedicate certain GPU pools for embeddings with large micro-batches and others for low-latency chat.
[08:36] Priya Menon: Could we have a hybrid — dedicated for chat, hosted for embeddings?
[08:40] Marcus Patel: Absolutely. Smart routing can split traffic by route, region, or cost. Redwood supports policy-based routing and automatic fallback.
[08:48] Lena Ortiz: Time check — still have ~30 mins, let's dig into the token math a bit and then cover pilot proposal.
[08:55] [09:05] Marcus Patel: I'll walk through a simplified unit econ table verbally: base decode cost per token depends on model FLOPs and GPU type; for our sample small LLM the raw decode might be X, translating to hosted $0.0011 / token. Add caching = multiply by (1 - cache_hit_rate). Batching reduces per-token GPU overhead; if batch efficiency raises from 0.6 to 0.9 you reduce cost by ~33%.
[09:30] Priya Menon: Can you explain batch efficiency a bit more?
[09:33] Marcus Patel: Sure — batch efficiency is how well the GPU footprint is utilized per request. If many small requests combine into a large batch, the amortized cost per token is lower. But you trade off latency because you sometimes wait for requests to arrive. We tune continuous batching to balance target latency SLOs.
[09:48] Carlos Ruiz: What's a realistic cache hit rate for a conversational app with shared system prompts?
[09:53] Marcus Patel: If you have a templated system message and repeated context, 10–30% is reasonable. If you de-duplicate heavy retrieval content via pre-processing, you can push that higher.
[10:05] Priya Menon: We're also experimenting with vector-store cold vs warm retrieval — hot retrievals might be cached at the app layer too.
[10:10] Marcus Patel: Exactly — app-level caching + model prefix caching compound.
[10:14] [11:00] Aisha Khan: Security Q: if we use public hosted but restrict region to EU, how locked down is the data path? Is it multi-tenant memory?
[11:07] Marcus Patel: Hosted in-region still is multi-tenant but with strong isolation in software; we don't mix workloads on the same VM-level instance for customer isolation but underlying GPU pools are shared. For stricter guarantees choose Dedicated or Private. We'll include a short doc on our tenancy model.
[11:23] Priya Menon: For committed dedicated, what's the contract length and how flexible are rollouts?
[11:28] Lena Ortiz: Typically monthly or annual commitments; rollouts can be canaryed — Redwood Console supports traffic splits and automatic fallback to hosted if capacity hits thresholds.
[11:37] Marcus Patel: And cost math for dedicated assumes a utilization target; if actual utilization is lower you pay more per effective token. We'll show a utilization sensitivity chart.
[11:47] [12:00] Carlos Ruiz: Priya — are you leaning hosted-first or do you want to go private?
[12:05] Priya Menon: I'd like a hosted-first pilot to validate quality and caching, but we need the path to private or dedicated if costs or residency force it.
[12:14] Lena Ortiz: That aligns with what we recommend: start hosted pilot with EU region, measure real cache hit and latency, then model dedicated economics for a committed deployment.
[12:24] [15:00] Marcus Patel: I'll add one more data point — quantization to 4-bit can reduce memory and perf cost significantly on compatible models, but there can be accuracy regressions. Redwood Optimize runs eval suites to estimate quality delta. For chat with sensitive outputs, do evals on your prompt sets.
[15:20] Priya Menon: Could you do a quick back-of-envelope for our numbers? 400M tokens / month, hosted at $0.0011, caching 20% and batch efficiency improvement 10%.
[15:33] Marcus Patel: Quick: baseline cost = 400M * $0.0011 = $440k / month. With 20% cache hit, payable tokens = 320M -> $352k. If batching efficiency improvement reduces unit by ~10% -> $317k. Dedicated might be $160–240k depending on utilization and quant. This is rough. We'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet.
[16:00] Carlos Ruiz: Those hosted numbers feel high for us; we'd need dedicated or hybrid to meet finance's target.
[16:06] Lena Ortiz: Understood. We'll show a 3-scenario comparison with conservative/worst/best assumptions so you can take to finance.
[16:15] [20:00] Aisha Khan: A security nuance — if private deploy is on-prem, what about patching and runtime updates? Who is responsible?
[20:07] Marcus Patel: On-prem/private has options: fully managed by Redwood with supported updates, or customer-managed with our tooling. Managed mode has a support fee but reduces ops burden. We'll include options and rough costs.
[20:25] Priya Menon: Great. For the pilot, what telemetry will you surface so we can measure hit rates and tail latency?
[20:30] Marcus Patel: Console provides per-token cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, cache hit metrics, and token-level trace for failed requests. We can instrument custom traces too.
[20:40] [25:00] Lena Ortiz: Ok, next I'd like to define a minimal pilot: 2–4 weeks, EU-hosted small scale (mirror your peak ~10–20 qps), include caching on, target p95 < 300ms for pilot, collect cache hit metrics and token volumes. Marcus — can you propose pilot scope and acceptance criteria?
[25:14] Marcus Patel: Proposed pilot: 14 days, replicate key routes (chat, retrieval), collect metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, cache hit rate, per-token costs, and model quality pass-rate on a small eval set. Acceptance criteria: p95 under 300ms in region, cost per effective token < $0.0010 baseline after caching.
[25:36] Priya Menon: That sounds reasonable to finance.
[25:40] Carlos Ruiz: What do you need from our side to start pilot?
[25:43] Marcus Patel: A traffic sample (1–2 days logs), your prompt set for evals, and an allowlist of test users. Also billing contact to set up trial credits.
[25:55] Priya Menon: I'll circulate those.
[26:00] [30:00] Lena Ortiz: We're hitting 30 min mark — any other pressing questions?
[30:06] Priya Menon: One more — are there middleware hooks or function-tool calling support? We plan to call internal APIs from model responses.
[30:12] Marcus Patel: Yes, Redwood supports structured outputs and tool-calling patterns; we can also enforce token limits and structured schema outputs to reduce downstream parsing cost.
[30:25] Aisha Khan: For SSO and audit logs, we need a SOC2 artifact and an architecture diagram for private deployment for our security review.
[30:33] Lena Ortiz: We'll include SOC2 attestation and a private deployment network diagram in the follow-up.
[30:40] [35:00] Marcus Patel: Quick note on fallback — if dedicated is saturated we can automatically route to hosted and apply cost accounting so you only pay hosted rates for overflow. That can be part of an HA plan.
[35:15] Carlos Ruiz: Good to know.
[35:20] [40:00] Priya Menon: Ok wrapping up — timeline expectations? If we get the pilot scope by next week can we start in two weeks?
[40:08] Marcus Patel: Yes, pilot start in two weeks is feasible. We need your traffic sample and an internal contact for setup.
[40:15] Lena Ortiz: I'll send the pricing spreadsheet and pilot checklist today. Marcus will run perf estimates and sample quant profiles. Priya will send traffic logs.
[40:25] [45:00] Carlos Ruiz: One final off-script — are there reference customers in EU with similar workloads you can point to?
[40:33] Lena Ortiz: We can share anonymized case studies and a reference intro with permission; will include in follow-up.
[40:40] Priya Menon: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[40:43] Marcus Patel: Thanks all.
[40:45] Lena Ortiz: Great — we'll follow up with the items discussed. Meeting adjourned.
[40:50] (recording ends)
